bull.b: Long-term agreements with established aerospace suppliers (Astronics, Hyundai WIA, Honeywell, Aciturri) materially de-risk design-to-production transition. A broad, contracted supply base supports certification-conforming builds, lowers single-supplier risk and strengthens manufacturability for scaled production.

Regulator-backed piloted transition flights, expanded flight permits and additional prototypes mark a shift from demonstration to certification-focused work. These milestones improve regulatory engagement, evidence of aircraft performance, and readiness for Critical Design Review—essential durable steps toward eventual commercial service.

Access to substantial financing plus ~$96M cash (≈12 months runway noted) and a large pre-order backlog underpin the firm's ability to fund certification and early industrialisation. This combination supports near-term program execution and preserves the option to convert pre-orders into future aircraft sales and recurring service revenue.

bear.b: Persistent negative equity and a sharp increase in debt materially limit financial flexibility. With 2025 debt exceeding assets, the company faces higher refinancing, covenant and creditor risks, raising the probability of dilution or restrictive financing terms that could delay industrialisation and commercialization.

Sustained negative operating and free cash flows indicate the business cannot self-fund development or scale production. Continued cash burn necessitates repeated external funding rounds, which strains strategic execution, increases dilution risk, and makes multi-year investment in certification and manufacturing contingent on capital markets.

Pushing target certification to 2029 extends the period before revenue generation and lengthens funded runway requirements. Delays increase execution risk, raise cumulative development costs, and prolong reliance on external financing, reducing near-term visibility into when scaled aircraft sales and recurring services will materialize.
